sourcePages.holdingText: The boundary between Canada and Newfoundland in the Labrador Peninsula is a line drawn due north from the eastern boundary of the bay or harbour of Ance Sablon as far as the fifty-second degree of north latitude, and from thence westward along that parallel until it reaches the Romaine river, and then northward along the left or east bank of that river and its head waters to their source and from thence due north to the crest of the watershed or height of land there, and from thence westward and northward along the crest of the watershed of the rivers flowing into the Atlantic Ocean until it reaches Cape Chidley.

input.text: The boundary between Canada and Newfoundland in the Labrador Peninsula is a line drawn due north from the eastern boundary of the bay or harbour of Ance Sablon as far as the fifty-second degree of north latitude, and from thence westward along that parallel until it reaches the Romaine river, and then northward along the left or east bank of that river and its head waters to their source and from thence due north to the crest of the watershed or height of land there, and from thence westward and northward along the crest of the watershed of the rivers flowing into the Atlantic Ocean until it reaches Cape Chidley.

claims: Term 2 of the British North America Act 1949 defines Newfoundland's province territory at Union as Newfoundland Island, adjacent islands, the Labrador coast as delimited by the 1 March 1927 Judicial Committee report approved 22 March 1927, and adjacent Labrador islands.

The 1927 Judicial Committee report's conclusion defines the Canada-Newfoundland line from Ance Sablon north to 52°N, west along that parallel to the Romaine River, north along its east bank/headwaters to their source, due north to the watershed, then along the Atlantic-river watershed to Cape Chidley.
Natural Resources Canada's separate Territorial Evolution, 1949 dataset says Newfoundland enters Confederation as the tenth province with boundaries as delimited in 1927.

The 1949 service grouping labels the Newfoundland feature within Canada (1949), and the local boundary question concerns an internal Canada provincial division when all Canadian service divisions are dissolved into Canada.

evidence.text: The British North America Act 1949, Schedule, Terms of Union, Term 2: “The Province of Newfoundland shall comprise the same territory as at the date of Union, that is to say, the island of Newfoundland and the islands adjacent thereto, the Coast of Labrador as delimited in the report delivered by the Judicial Committee of His Majesty's Privy Council on the first day of March, 1927, and approved by His Majesty in His Privy Council on the twenty-second day of March, 1927, and the islands adjacent to the said Coast of Labrador.”

1927 Judicial Committee report, conclusion: “the boundary between Canada and Newfoundland in the Labrador Peninsula is a line drawn due north from the eastern boundary of the bay or harbour of Ance Sablon as far as the fifty-second degree of north latitude, and from thence westward along that parallel until it reaches the Romaine river, and then northward along the left or east bank of that river and its head waters to their source and from thence due north to the crest of the watershed or height of land there, and from thence westward and northward along the crest of the watershed of the rivers flowing into the Atlantic Ocean until it reaches Cape Chidley”. Report delivered 1 March 1927.

Natural Resources Canada Open Data Portal, separate dataset “Territorial Evolution, 1949”: “In 1949, Newfoundland enters Confederation as the tenth province with the boundaries as delimited in 1927.” Publisher is Natural Resources Canada; licence is Open Government Licence - Canada.

English ArcGIS REST layer 8 attribute query where START_TIME=1949 returns Newfoundland with START_TIME 1949, END_TIME 1949, and Period_Group “Canada (1949)”. Filtered geometry query where START_TIME=1949 AND PROV_NAME='Newfoundland' returns a GeoJSON MultiPolygon for that feature.
